extracted.intended_audience: Federal Circuit judges, USPTO examiners, and patent practitioners (incl. pro se appellants)
extracted.subtask_description: A petition for panel rehearing and rehearing en banc challenging a Federal Circuit opinion and PTAB/USPTO rejections, focusing on claim construction, §101 eligibility, anticipation (§102), obviousness (§103), and reliance on PHOSITA evidence and prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: De novo claim construction when no fact findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction should be reviewed de novo where there are no fact findings implicated (citing Imes, Teva, Markman, Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel's failure to review claim construction de novo is reversible error; where nothing in the case implicates deference to fact findings, the court must independently determine ordinary meaning and scope of claim terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain words of the claims and prosecution interpretation control
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain language of the claims, together with the inventor's interpretation during prosecution, must be given effect and cannot be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like “dosage” (here argued to mean a specified amount for administration) are limiting when specification, examples, tables, and prosecution statements show a specific meaning; examiner/court cannot treat such terms as non-limiting contrary to prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) must align with PHOSITA
rubrics_metrics.description: The BRI applied by the PTO/Board must be consistent with how a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) would understand the claim terms (In re Cortright).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim constructions that conflict with PHOSITA testimony or analogous patents are improper; BRI cannot be divorced from skilled-worker evidence on meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural limitations (e.g., 'intermixture') are substantive
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural recitations such as “intermixture of lipids from different sources” are structural limitations that can make a claimed composition a patentable 'composition of matter' rather than a product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural character (not mere discovery of a natural phenomenon) supports patent eligibility (citing Garnero, Gulack). The existence of an intermixture requirement precludes treating the claim as simply a natural product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution disclaimer binds claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecution statements or disclaimers (e.g., disclaiming a 'single source') are binding and must be considered when construing claims and assessing novelty/eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panel/Board must not ignore undisputed prosecution disclaimers; disclaimer that claims are not single-source impacts both §101 and §102 analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires the reference to necessarily practice the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference anticipates only if it necessarily discloses the claimed subject matter — it must function as claimed, not merely possibly or arguably (distinguishing §102 from §103 analyses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References that 'may' but do not necessarily disclose a limitation (e.g., specific dosages, casings providing controlled delivery, intermixture arranged as claimed) cannot be used to show anticipation; the Board may not 'fill in' missing limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board/examiner may not fill in missing claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTAB or examiner cannot supply missing claim elements or 'optimize' a prior-art reference to meet claim limitations (Nidec, Lindemann).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions that infer or invent unstated limitations in prior art to reach anticipation are improper; part-to-part relationships and specific arrangements must be present in the reference itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 analysis is separate from §§102/103
rubrics_metrics.description: The §101 patent-eligibility inquiry is distinct from novelty and obviousness analyses; one must not import §102/§103 reasoning wholesale into §101 (Mayo, Alice, Rapid, Classen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim language as a whole is not directed to an ineligible concept, the §101 inquiry ends; applying anticipation/novelty reasoning to eligibility is reversible error.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 step one: determine whether claim is directed to a patent-ineligible concept
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, the court asks whether the claim is directed to an ineligible concept (laws of nature, natural products, abstract ideas); if not, eligibility is satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features not found in nature (e.g., dosage limitations, casings providing controlled delivery, intermixtures) can take a claim out of the realm of natural products at step one—no further 'inventive concept' analysis is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: §101 step two: 'inventive concept' as 'significantly more' when required
rubrics_metrics.description: If step one points to a patent-ineligible concept, step two asks whether the claimed elements, individually or as an ordered combination, add an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter (Mayo/Alice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must consider the claims 'on the whole' (Diehr, Rapid) and evaluate whether limitations like controlled dosage, controlled delivery casings, and specified intermixtures confer significantly more than a natural law/product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional printed matter or instructions should not be conflated with natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional or instructional aspects combined with an alleged natural product should not automatically cause the claim to be characterized as a natural product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims include functional structure (e.g., casings that control delivery) those functional structures may contribute to eligibility rather than render the claim ineligible as a mere natural product.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary meaning of claim terms determined de novo in temporal context
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary meaning of claim terms should be determined as a matter of law, de novo, and in the temporal context of the application (Markman, Phillips, Teva).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must interpret terms like 'lipid', 'source', and 'dosage' according to their plain and contextual meaning at the time of filing, not by later-evolved or strained interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of evidence and burden to prove anticipation/enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO/Board carries the burden to prove anticipation or lack of enablement by a preponderance of the evidence; gaps or inconclusive data in a reference defeat anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where references lack enabling disclosure of critical limitations (e.g., specific dosages, age-specific dosing), the Board cannot establish anticipation; courts must review whether the evidentiary showing meets the burden (Oetiker, Perricone).

rubrics_metrics.name: Part-to-part arrangement and 'arranged as in the claim' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art reference must disclose the part-to-part relationships and arrangement 'as in the claim' to anticipate; mere disclosure of components is insufficient (Nidec, Lindemann).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References that list components or ranges but do not teach the claimed intermixture, dosage arrangement, or casing-delivery relationship cannot be held to anticipate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of scientific evidence and PHOSITA testimony for structural/functional differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific publications and PHOSITA declarations showing that extraction, mixing, or encapsulation materially change physical/chemical properties are relevant to novelty and eligibility and must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical evidence that manipulated mixtures have properties not found in nature supports non-natural character of claimed compositions and undercuts conclusions that claims are indistinguishable from natural products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be considered 'as a whole' for eligibility and cannot be dissected
rubrics_metrics.description: The eligibility inquiry requires considering the claimed combination in its entirety rather than excising or ignoring limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excising limitations such as 'providing controlled delivery' or 'dosage' from the analysis (i.e., 'mutilating the claims') is improper and may render the analysis legally deficient (Gulack, Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecution and examiner admissions about lack of natural counterpart are highly relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions in the prosecution record or by the examiner that there is no naturally occurring counterpart to claimed combinations are significant evidence of structural distinction from natural products (Myriad, Chakrabarty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such admissions should weigh against treating the claim as directed to a natural product; they support eligibility if the claimed combination has no natural counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art must enable claimed limitations (e.g., 'dosage') to anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement in the prior art is required for anticipation; a reference’s mere disclosure of ranges or non-specific data does not necessarily enable specific dosage limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference that does not teach how to achieve the claimed dosage for relevant populations or contexts cannot be relied upon to anticipate—enablement and functional disclosure matter (Perricone, Elsner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to address arguments may amount to conceding them
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellate decision that fails to address significant arguments or evidence may be treated as having conceded those issues (Herrmann, Soni).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should explicitly address dispositive arguments and evidence; unexplained affirmances of Board findings without analysis may be inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of post-filing scientific publications and expert declarations can corroborate inventive concept and public-health importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific studies and expert declarations showing that claimed formulations solve long-felt problems, alter properties, or have large public-health benefits are relevant to demonstrating the significance and nonobviousness/importance of an invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not dispositive of eligibility, substantial corroborating scientific evidence and PHOSITA testimony should be weighed in assessing whether claimed subject matter adds 'significantly more' or is structurally distinct from natural products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims reciting dosage, controlled delivery, and specified ratios can confer patent-eligibility or inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that combines formulation, explicit dosage limitations, casings that provide controlled delivery, and specified intermixture ratios may be sufficiently distinct from natural products and confer eligibility or an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should recognize combinations of structural and functional limitations (e.g., dosage + controlled delivery + intermixture) as potentially patent-eligible without collapsing the analysis into novelty or obviousness reexamination.
